item.title: World shares are mixed as Nvidia's troubles weigh on AI stocks
item.description: World shares were mixed on Thursday as concerns over leadership at chipmaker Nvidia weighed on artificial intelligence-related stocks.
item.dc:creator: The Associated Press
item.content:encoded: NEW YORK — The U.S. stock market shook Thursday, but it largely absorbed big swings for Nvidia and oil prices and finished with relatively modest losses. The moves suggested Wall Street sees limited fallout for the artificial intelligence industry, which carries immense influence on the market, despite the sudden fall of one of its biggest evangelists. After dropping nearly one per cent at the start of trading, the S&P 500 quickly erased all of the loss before finishing with a dip of 0.4 per cent. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 189 points, or 0.4 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite sank 0.4 per cent after trimming an early drop of 1.6 per cent. Stocks broadly felt pressure from a rise in oil prices after U.S. President Donald Trump said he’s no longer interested in a deal with Iran to end their war. Instead of that, Trump said he asked his vice president to investigate U.S. cities and states run by Democrats. On a typical day, that could be the main driver of action on Wall Street. But little has been typical recently for the yo-yoing stock market. The focus instead was on Nvidia’s stock. It plunged 14 per cent at the start of trading following the resignation of Jensen Huang, its CEO, co-founder and face of the brand. The chip company’s stock has been sinking since its board announced an investigation into Huang for a relationship with a woman suspected of being a Chinese government agent. It’s a stunning fall for Huang and for Nvidia, which had become Wall Street’s most valuable and influential stock because of its central role in the AI boom. Its stock price set a record last month after soaring an astounding 1,722 per cent in four years. That compares with the already healthy gain of nearly 109 per cent for the overall S&P 500 over the same time. But Nvidia’s price dropped 27 per cent from then through Wednesday. At first, the drop was because of worries about too-high prices for stocks across the AI industry. More recently, it’s been due to worries about whether Huang would remain as CEO and how Nvidia would navigate a future without him. Nvidia’s board answered the first question Thursday morning, when it said Huang resigned, and it named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as its interim CEO. The second question remains unanswered. And it looms over the entire market because Nvidia and the broader AI industry have been the main reasons the U.S. stock market has set so many records in recent years. Nvidia, to be sure, is still selling AI chips at a quick rate regardless of who stands on a stage and talks them up, and analysts said it remains the industry’s leader. That helped Nvidia quickly halve its early loss Thursday, and its stock finished with a fall of 4.3 per cent. That paring helped the broader market to recover. Outside of Nvidia, stocks across the AI industry swung in the uncertainty. CoreWeave, which buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them to customers over the cloud, fell 6.9 per cent. Micron Technology, which sells memory for computers that’s been getting gobbled up in the AI frenzy, sank 1.6 per cent. But Broadcom rose 5.5 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices added 5.9 per cent on hopes the rival chip companies will gain a competitive advantage. Those two gains came close to offsetting the drop for Nvidia, which was the single heaviest weight on the S&P 500. That suggests investors see the AI business expanding to other players rather than depending solely on Nvidia. Also helping to limit the U.S. market’s losses were gains for stocks in the oil and gas industry. Marathon Petroleum climbed 2.5 per cent, and ExxonMobil added 1.8 per cent. They benefited from a rise in oil prices after Trump said on his social media platform, “We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!” The price for a barrel of Brent crude climbed 3.3 per cent to US$95.82. The price for the most actively traded contract in the Brent market has been veering sharply since the United States and Israel began the war with Iran in late February, bouncing between roughly US$70 and US$120. Higher oil prices push up worries about inflation, and the yield on the 10-year Treasury jumped to 5.12 per cent from 4.98 per cent late Tuesday. Trading in the bond market had been closed Wednesday for Veterans Day. Higher yields make borrowing money more expensive for everyone, from the U.S. government to companies building AI data centres to regular people buying houses. High mortgage rates helped send sales of previously occupied U.S. homes in October to their slowest pace in more than 16 years. The housing industry has been slowing the U.S. economy but not upending it. A separate report on Thursday said that slightly more U.S. workers applied for unemployment benefits last week, but the number remains relatively low compared with history. All told, the S&P 500 fell 26.98 points to 7,592.40. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dipped 189.40 to 52,297.09, and the Nasdaq composite sank 100.10 to 25,366.09. In stock markets abroad, indexes were mixed in Europe following a weaker finish in Asia. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1.3 per cent for one of the world’s biggest moves. ___ Stan Choe, The Associated Press AP Business Writer Yuri Kageyama contributed to this report.

item.title: Canada-U.S. travel turnoff reversing after U.S. midterm elections
item.description: Travel experts say the Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory is poised to fan a trend of rising Canadian visitor volumes to the United States.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: MONTREAL — The Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory is poised to fan a trend of rising Canadian visitor volumes to the United States, counteracting the effect of the recent trade war flare-up, travel experts say. Canadian return trips from America rose three per cent in October compared with the same period last year, the seventh-straight month of growth, according to preliminary figures from Statistics Canada. However, the increase marked a smaller uptick than the levels seen through much of the summer and into September. At Flight Centre Travel Group Canada, new leisure bookings — distinct from trips taken — fell 26 per cent year-over-year last month in response to a fresh round of tariffs and taunts by U.S. President Donald Trump weeks earlier. “It really just shows you how fragile cross-border travel is, specifically from the leisure market,” said Amra Durakovic, a spokesperson for the travel agency. Over the past week though, Flight Centre has seen signs of a return to the Canada-U.S. tourism rebound in the wake of the Democrats’ electoral success on Nov. 3, widely viewed as a rebuke to White House policies. “We are hearing a degree of cautious optimism from some travellers who were reluctant to return,” Durakovic said. “One customer, he booked a Mississippi River cruise, and they did that instead of exploring another European holiday,” she said. “Tuesday’s election, that influenced their decision. They said that they definitely feel a lot more comfortable travelling to the U.S. now.” For now, Canadian visitor volumes remain far below levels from 2024 — 27 per cent below in October — as the trade war drags on and Canadians opt for other destinations. Nonetheless, the torrent of votes for Democratic candidates from Kansas to the Carolinas set off flickers of a possible revival in stateside travel, or perhaps signs of what a Democratic triumph in 2028 could herald for tourism. “Pickup to the U.S. has happened in the last week — people that weren’t going to go,” said Marty Firestone, noting an abrupt rise in business at the insurance firm he heads, Travel Secure Inc. “There was a real bad feeling last year: ‘I’m not going there. That man doesn’t want us. He calls us the 51st state,’” Firestone said, describing the attitude of many Canadians. “With the Democratic blue tsunami, as they call it, I think that Canadians are somewhat feeling a little more relieved about going back to the U.S.” Others say it’s too early to gauge whether the midterms revamped interest in cross-border trips. “We need at least a month,” said Richard Vanderlubbe, who heads Hamilton-based travel agency Tripcentral.ca. Even if an upward shift is underway, he suspects it’s a minor one, with Trump set to remain in the Oval Office for two more years. “I don’t feel like there’s a sea change. It’s not like the phones lit up on Wednesday morning with emails flying and, ‘Hey, OK, it’s good to go to the States now.’” The ill feeling is strong enough that some travel agencies avoid promoting American packages altogether. “We just don’t know which of our customers is going to be wildly offended by any kind of marketing in the United States … so we just don’t do it,” Vanderlubbe said. “To market the U.S. is like dynamite.” Flight volumes from Canada to Florida, Arizona, Nevada and California are down 17 per cent in total this quarter versus the final three months of 2024, according to aviation data firm Cirium. Overall Canada-U.S. flight volumes decreased only 10 per cent, revealing the bigger drop in demand for sun-splashed leisure hot spots. Corporate travel continues to hum along, Durakovic said, with virtually no drop in Flight Centre bookings over the past couple of years. “It’s still business as usual. You can’t exactly stop travelling to the U.S. because of politics,” she said. The broader Canadian aversion to travelling south of the border combined with the shutdown of Cuban resorts amid a fuel shortage caused by an American oil blockade has pushed sun seekers farther afield. Mexico, the Dominican Republic and Jamaica have surged in popularity, travel agents said. Portugal and Spain have also enjoyed a recent boost in Canadian visitors. “Air Transat flights to Malaga are full,” said Sal Lato, who owns the Voyages Marlin travel agency franchise. Meanwhile, the leisure airline has cut the 36 flights a week it operated between Canada and Florida in late 2024 down to zero. Not all winter escapees can simply point their finger at a fresh spot on the map and jet off for a getaway, extended or otherwise. “There are still deep ties to many U.S. snowbird destinations,” said Stephen Fine, founder of Snowbird Advisor Insurance. “They have friends who’ve been going there for years and they want to be able to spend their winters with that community,” he said of many Canadians. “A lot of them own properties there. People want to drive down to their destination or have their vehicles with them for the winter,” he noted. For them, America may be the only option. --- Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press This report by The Canadian Press was first published Nov. 12, 2026.

item.title: Investor Outlook: Nvidia’s AI demand offers cushion after Huang’s exit
item.description: Nvidia faces a leadership transition as Kim Forrest discusses the chipmaker’s next chapter and the implications for AI stocks.
item.dc:creator: BNN Bloomberg
item.content:encoded: Jensen Huang’s departure puts Nvidia’s next chapter in focus, raising questions about how the AI chipmaker will evolve under new leadership. BNN Bloomberg spoke with Kim Forrest, founder and chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners, about the transition and what it could mean for the semiconductor sector. Key Takeaways Read the full transcript below: ROGER: Nvidia shares are under pressure with the news that CEO Jensen Huang is resigning amid allegations surrounding a second extramarital affair. Investors are now grappling with what leadership uncertainty could mean for one of the world’s most valuable companies, possibly one of the most powerful companies, a leader in the AI race. Joining us now is Kim Forrest, founder and chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners. Kim, thanks very much for joining us today. KIM: It’s a pleasure. ROGER: OK, we’re seeing the reaction, but the — it seems to be tempered a little bit, a little more now. I mean, earlier today, when the news first broke on the — on the premarket, it was down about 10 per cent. Now we’re off about 4.8, 4.9. How are people approaching this? How are you approaching it? KIM: Well, I think you really have to look at how big of a company we’re talking about here. It’s not a one-person company. That is the good news. The other thing is, is this is one of the companies that’s supplying AI. It is a huge driver, of course, of everything AI. But again, the companies who are buying their products are the ones that are sort of driving where the product goes, not the company driving where the models go. So if you look at it that way, and you realize that their production is sold out a year ahead of time, you have relatively low risk here for the company not meeting its financial objectives. It also looks like there is a bench of people that can take over, at least in the interim. And I think it’ll be interesting who the board picks as the next CEO. Nvidia has always been a very narrow company. First, for most of its life, it did video, you know, chips, and now it has branched out into other areas that use that technology in different ways. So what could Nvidia become? Only the next CEO knows. ROGER: There is — there is a lot ahead. Now you mentioned that it’s more than just Huang’s Nvidia, but he was perceived as a rock star and kind of — and he’s the face of it. And he had that unique arrangement. I mean, 60 people reported directly to him. Is that — are those things easy to overcome? KIM: Well, we’re going to find out. But look at his schedule. I think that gives you a peek into what the company was really doing. He has been doing a lot of press, a lot of conferences, flying around the world. That’s some of the issues that probably got him into the trouble that he’s in. That he wasn’t back at the company, you know, minding the store. So I’m thinking that the company probably is well positioned internally to do what it does, which is make the chip that every AI frontier lab wants to have. And I think that is important for investors to remember whenever they see the stock price falling. ROGER: OK, now for a replacement, we’ve got Colette Kress, temporary. The CFO is now in as CEO. Is she a possibility, or will they look outside, do you think? KIM: Well, the company itself has said internal and external candidates are being looked at, and I believe she has a pretty good shot at retaining that. Now we will certainly see, and I think the board, because it doesn’t look great for them that these issues have come up, and it doesn’t sound like they were really on top of, you know, being a board of directors, knowing what the management is doing, so I think they’re going to be very careful about who they choose as CEO. Although they have to really start getting down to the work here shortly. ROGER: And I want to ask: They also appointed Harvey Jones as the chair, and they’ve never had a chair before. What does that — does that mean anything to you, or is it — can we read into it? KIM: Well, absolutely. I mean, you know, Jensen Huang was the company. He was the chairman of the board. He was the CEO, and, you know, in a lot of governance circles, that is a warning sign that there’s too much power in one person. So I think it’s good that they did not, you know, keep that arrangement. But I don’t think it’s practical either. So I think having a separated CEO and board chair is probably what a lot of companies should think about doing, and just spread the risk around and make people more accountable. ROGER: All right, just doing some quick math. Down about 17 per cent. Is Nvidia a buying opportunity, or is it AMD or something like that? KIM: Well, I think a lot of companies are. I’m a bull on the longer-term aspects of AI. I am somebody who doesn’t believe that the leading frontier labs are going to be game over, the winners in the long run. So I think there is a lot of opportunity out there, and we like to spread the risk around and not just have one holding being the AI chip. So we like AMD, we like Micron and we like Nvidia. ROGER: Any concerns about the chips from a government perspective, that they may put in restriction or further restrictions on what — who can buy the chips, what, when and where? KIM: Well, I think everybody’s going to take a good, hard look at that. So yes, I would think that there are some — we’ll just say clarifications coming to the export laws, especially in these — in AI chips. ROGER: All right, and you mentioned the numbers are pretty solid. What are you going to be looking for next week with that — that earnings report? What will be a key number for you? KIM: Well, it’s really what the bookings are going to be, you know, beyond a year ahead. What do the bookings look like? You know, we’ve been using this as a measure of: Is AI healthy? Looking at the semiconductors, things are turning. I think Anthropic, with it being public, is going to be the new face of AI health. Are people buying their product, which is a service to do, you know, whatever they do with it, write code, you know, create agents, whatever? So I think the importance of Nvidia being the indicator of health in AI spending is going to change, and I think that’s probably a good thing. ROGER: OK, we have to wrap it up there, Kim. But always appreciate talking to you. Thanks very much for joining us. KIM: Thank you. ROGER: Kim Forrest, founder and chief investment officer at Bokeh Capital Partners. --- This BNN Bloomberg summary and transcript of the Nov. 12, 2026 interview with Kim Forrest are published with the assistance of AI. Original research, interview questions and added context was created by BNN Bloomberg journalists. An editor also reviewed this material before it was published to ensure its accuracy and adherence with BNN Bloomberg editorial policies and standards.

item.title: Investors worry the AI trade might lose Nvidia’s largesse after Huang
item.description: As chip giant Nvidia’s chief Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday, investors’ biggest fears were as much about the future of the multitrillion-dollar company as its ability and willingness to ...
item.dc:creator: Reuters Staff
item.content:encoded: SINGAPORE -- As chip giant Nvidia’s chief Jensen Huang stepped down on Thursday, investors’ biggest fears were as much about the future of the multitrillion-dollar company as its ability and willingness to continue bankrolling the AI boom. Huang’s exit is yet another pressure point on the global markets’ most crowded trade and came after the board of the world’s dominant chipmaker, at the cutting edge of computing, met late on Wednesday to decide the longtime CEO’s fate after reports of his two extramarital affairs. The company said Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will take over as interim CEO as Nvidia looks for a permanent successor. Traders’ first reaction was to punish Nvidia shares and those of its customers, including data-centre firms CoreWeave and Naver, while pushing shares of chipmaking rivals Broadcom and AMD higher. Shares in China’s leading makers of graphics processing units (GPUs) surged, as the leadership upheaval at Nvidia boosted expectations that local chip suppliers could win greater market share. Moore Threads, MetaX and Cambricon all jumped nearly 10 per cent. Nvidia shares pared premarket losses but were still down nearly five per cent at 1600 GMT. The worry in the market is that the stakes are far higher and that if Nvidia — under a different leader — backs away from a strategy of financing data centers, then the AI boom itself loses momentum. “Nvidia has been called the ‘Bank of AI.’ They’ll sell you the chips and loan you the money. If they have to take a step back because of what’s going on, will that cut off funding to smaller companies that need it? That’s an open question,” said Joe Saluzzi, partner and co-head of equity trading at Themis Trading in Chatham, New Jersey. Nvidia has been the banner stock of the AI revolution, with its chip technology ahead of rivals and enormous sales driving the share price up some 900 per cent over the four years since the launch of OpenAI’s ChatGPT ushered in the AI era. But Nvidia has also become a torchbearer and financier, anticipating demand for ever more powerful chips while sinking billions of dollars into funding its own customers via a mix of equity investments and other promises. “Nvidia’s credit support is what makes much of this debt finance-able across the AI hyperscaler deal front,” said Christopher Brown, senior vice president, investments, at Synovus Securities. “Lenders will ask what happens to that support if Nvidia’s leadership or regulatory standing is impaired, and Nvidia’s own willingness to extend more guarantees may be constrained.” Nvidia’s board launched an investigation into Huang following reports he had an extramarital affair with a businesswoman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy. A subsequent report about another affair came out ahead of Wednesday’s board meeting. Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Equities, said Nvidia’s revenue would not suddenly plunge after Huang’s exit and, therefore, the bigger concern was about the future, given Huang was the person with the vision for computing. “Replacing that strategic vision ... is an enormous challenge,” he said. Nvidia sinks and takes some, but not all, along Huang’s departure leaves a vacuum at the top of the roughly US$4 trillion chipmaker that he co-founded and built over more than three decades to become the top supplier of chips and the nexus of the U.S.-China technology rivalry. Chipmakers in Asia, whose stocks have soared with Nvidia and the AI spending boom, but lately sagged on worries about funding costs and the demand outlook, slipped. Nvidia listed $164.5 billion in financial commitments in its most recent earnings report, with an obligation capped at $105 billion on an OpenAI data centre in Ohio and lease and other capacity guarantees topping $50 billion. In August, it said it had partnered with six major financial institutions including Apollo, BlackRock and Blackstone to launch compute financing platforms aimed at raising over $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure. Huang said then the company had the option to backstop up to $125 billion, or 25 per cent of the potential deals. “The interlocking deals that Nvidia has with so much of the industry raises the question into whether that created more stability or more fragility,” said Steve Sosnick, chief market analyst at Interactive Brokers in Connecticut. Nvidia is also one of the investors in Claude chatbot creator Anthropic’s initial public offering. The listing this month is set to serve as a test of investor appetite for all things AI. Shares in Nvidia-backed data-centre operator CoreWeave, which surged on Wednesday on upbeat earnings, fell more than six per cent. Shares in South Korea’s Naver, in which Nvidia took a $1 billion stake by financing a data-center expansion, also dropped six per cent. To be sure, investors said, the quality of Nvidia’s products is not likely to change, and change at the top won’t quickly hit demand. “Nvidia’s core asset is its advanced GPUs, which still have no real substitute in the market,” said Anna Wu, founder of Floodlines Research. “The AI trade rests on that demand, not on one individual.” But when the company reports earnings next week, the focus will inevitably be on leadership, strategy and whether a sales outlook formed under Huang still holds up under a successor. (Reporting by Ankur Banerjee in Singapore, Tom Westbrook in Sydney, Prathik Jayaprakash, Anhata Rooprai, Lakshmi Tharuniyaa, Johann Cherian in Bengaluru and Li Gu in Shanghai; Editing by Thomas Derpinghaus, Vidya Ranganathan, Mark Potter and Emelia Sithole-Matarise)
